content: Zinc is a metallic chemical element represented by the symbol Zn and has an atomic number of 30. Historically, it has also been referred to as spelter in certain contexts, such as sculpture and metallurgy. Zinc is a moderately reactive metal with a blue-gray appearance. When exposed to moist air, it tarnishes, and when burned in air, it produces a bright bluish-green flame, releasing zinc oxide fumes. It reacts with acids, alkalis, and other non-metals. Impure zinc reacts with dilute acids to release hydrogen gas. Zinc predominantly exhibits an oxidation state of +2. Between 100°C and 210°C (212°F to 410°F), zinc is malleable and can be shaped easily. However, above 210°C (410°F), it becomes brittle and can be pulverized. Zinc is nonmagnetic. Zinc plays a critical biological role as an essential element required for sustaining life. Approximately 3,000 proteins in the human body contain zinc prosthetic groups, including zinc fingers, which are structural motifs in proteins. Over a dozen types of human cells secrete zinc ions, and the medical and health-related roles of these secreted zinc signals are under active investigation. Zinc ions are now recognized as neurotransmitters. Cells in the salivary gland, prostate, immune system, and intestine are among those that secrete zinc. Zinc also acts as an activator for certain enzymes, such as carbonic anhydrase, which is vital for carbon dioxide transport in vertebrate blood. In plants, zinc is necessary for leaf formation, the synthesis of indole acetic acid (auxin), and anaerobic respiration (alcoholic fermentation). Zinc is found in various food sources, including oysters, animal proteins, beans, nuts, almonds, whole grains, pumpkin seeds, and sunflower seeds. Turkey neck and beef cuts like chuck or shank also contain significant amounts of zinc. However, phytates, present in whole grain breads, cereals, legumes, and other products, can reduce zinc absorption. Clinical studies suggest that zinc, combined with antioxidants, may slow the progression of age-related macular degeneration. Additionally, significant dietary zinc intake has been shown to delay the onset of influenza. Soil conservation studies analyze the uptake of naturally occurring zinc by plants in different soil types. The recommended dietary allowance (RDA) for zinc in the United States is 11 mg per day for males and 8 mg per day for females, with higher amounts recommended during pregnancy and lactation. Zinc deficiency occurs due to inadequate dietary intake or poor absorption of zinc. Symptoms of zinc deficiency include hair loss, skin lesions, diarrhea, and wasting of body tissues. Zinc is also associated with functions such as eyesight, taste, smell, and memory, and its deficiency can impair these functions. Congenital abnormalities leading to zinc deficiency can result in a condition called acrodermatitis enteropathica. Ensuring sufficient zinc intake during pregnancy and early childhood is crucial, as zinc deficiency can impair brain development in utero and during youth. Zinc deficiency has also been linked to acne and leukonychia (white spots on fingernails), which may indicate insufficient zinc levels. Zinc deficiency has been implicated as a potential cause of anorexia nervosa (AN). A lack of zinc reduces appetite, which can lead to anorexia nervosa. Appetite disorders, in turn, cause malnutrition, including inadequate zinc intake. Since 1979, zinc supplementation has been proposed as a treatment for anorexia nervosa. At least 15 clinical trials have demonstrated that zinc supplementation improves weight gain in individuals with anorexia. A 1994 randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial showed that 14 mg of zinc per day doubled the rate of body mass increase in anorexia nervosa patients. Deficiencies in other nutrients, such as tyrosine, tryptophan (precursors of norepinephrine and serotonin), and vitamin B1 (thiamine), may also contribute to malnutrition-induced malnutrition. While zinc is essential for health, excessive zinc intake can be harmful. Overabsorption of zinc can suppress the absorption of other essential minerals, such as copper and iron. Free zinc ions in solution are highly toxic to plants, invertebrates, and even vertebrate fish. The Free Ion Activity Model (FIAM) demonstrates that micromolar concentrations of free zinc ions can be lethal to some organisms. For example, a concentration of 6 micromolar zinc killed 93% of Daphnia in water. Ingesting excessive zinc, such as from U.S. pennies minted after 1982, can cause severe hemolytic anemia in dogs, often leading to death. Zinc is also highly toxic to pet parrots, and poisoning is frequently fatal. Copper deficiency can be induced at zinc intake levels as low as 100–300 mg/day. The USDA RDA for zinc is 15 mg/day. Zinc salts are effective against pathogens when applied directly. Zinc ingestion significantly reduces the severity of gastroenteritis, possibly due to the antimicrobial action of zinc ions in the gastrointestinal tract or their absorption and subsequent release by immune cells, such as granulocytes. Clinical trials have shown that zinc gluconate and zinc gluconate glycine (used in lozenges) can shorten the duration of common cold symptoms. The glycine content in these formulations can vary from two to twenty moles per mole of zinc gluconate. Zinc oxide is one of the most well-known and widely used zinc compounds, serving as a base for white pigments in paint. It is also used industrially in the rubber industry and as an opaque sunscreen. Other zinc compounds, such as zinc chloride (used in deodorants), zinc pyrithione (found in anti-dandruff shampoos), zinc sulfide (used in luminescent paints), and zinc methyl or zinc diethyl (used in organic laboratories), have various industrial applications. Approximately one-quarter of all zinc production is consumed in the form of zinc compounds. Metallic zinc is not considered toxic, but free zinc ions in solution are highly toxic. Inhalation of freshly formed zinc oxide fumes, such as during the welding of galvanized materials, can cause a condition known as zinc shakes or zinc chills (a form of metal fume fever). Excessive zinc intake can also lead to deficiencies in other dietary minerals.
